newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish Protestants say truce still intact.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish Protestants say truce still intact.

text.p: Protestant politicians linked with pro-British Loyalist guerrillas, who face a threat of being expelled from Northern Ireland peace talks, said on Monday their extremist allies were still holding to a ceasefire.

Critics of the Loyalists among mainstream Protestant parties say they will press Britain at the talks, restarting on Monday after a New Year break, to state whether recent attacks on Roman Catholics have breached a 27-month-old truce declared by the Loyalists.

The critics say the Ulster Democratic Party (UDP) and Progressive Unionist Party (PUP), political wings of banned Loyalist guerrilla groups, must be expelled if it is established that the attacks were approved by the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC) which called a truce in October 1994.

"Our indications are...that the CLMC are still very much committed to their ceasefire and that they are very much committed to seeing a peaceful democratic resolution of the problems within Northern Ireland," UDP politician David Adams told BBC radio before the talks restarted.

The Loyalists want Northern Ireland to remain British. Sinn Fein, political wing of the guerrilla Irish Republican Army which is fighting for the province to be united with Ireland, is barred from the talks until the IRA reinstates a truce it ended last February with bombs on the British mainland.
The row has added a new layer of controversy to the Anglo-Irish sponsored peace talks which have been dogged by disputes and overshadowed by IRA violence since their launch last June.
Police chiefs blame Loyalist guerrillas for what they regard as revenge attacks after a surge in IRA activity but have not publicly linked the incidents to the CLMC.
Britain has warned Loyalists they could face expulsion but has so far resisted penalising them, saying that it believes the CLMC ceasefire is fragile but still in operation.

PUP leader David Ervine told BBC radio: "I think that Loyalism has been responsible for violence but the CLMC clearly are saying that their ceasefire is not over -- and that if it is over everybody will know about it."

Most of the parties at the talks believe the UDP and PUP have played a crucial part in restraining Loyalist militants in the face of IRA violence and that expulsion would weaken the politicians' influence with guerrilla hawks.
But Sinn Fein accuses Britain of double standards, saying London is bending over backwards to keep Loyalists at the table while keeping republicans outside.
Britain says IRA violence, not London's intransigence, is blocking Sinn Fein's entry to the talks.
